uncited: *   **Fine Grid Elements:** Vertices ($V_f$), Edges ($E_f$), and Quadrilaterals ($Q_f$).
*   **Coarse Grid Elements:** Vertices ($V_c$), Edges ($E_c$), and Quadrilaterals ($Q_c$).
*   **Stitch Cells:** The output geometry is defined by the vertices of the fine and coarse grids.

**Identify Boundary Elements:** For each fine grid embedded in a coarse grid, identify the fine grid elements that lie on the boundary of the fine grid region (i.e., those not fully contained within another finer grid).
*   **Deformed Triangle Prism:** If $Q_f$ connects to a coarse edge $E_c$ in one direction and a vertex or edge in the other.
*   **Edge Promotion:** An edge might be "upgraded" to a quadrilateral case if adjacent edges are refined.
*   **Vertex Promotion:** A fine vertex can be promoted to an edge if any of the coarse grid points 3, 5, or 6 (in a local canonical numbering) is refined.
*   **Triangular Prism Case:** If refined coarse points are replaced by fine edges.
*   **Refinement Ratios:** The method works with commonly used refinement ratios.
*   **Non-planar Boundaries:** 2D refinement configurations that produce subdivided quadrilaterals also yield non-planar cell boundaries.
An algorithm that utilizes stitching cells to construct an unstructured geometry across AMR levels to fill gaps between hierarchy levels.
It is used when re-sampling or using redundant coarse data is not feasible or desired.
*   **Time Complexity:** The complexity is linear with respect to the number of boundary elements between refinement levels.
The number of stitch cells generated is proportional to the surface area of the fine grids embedded in the coarse grid.
*   **Memory Complexity:** The memory usage is proportional to the number of stitch cells generated.
Each stitch cell stores references to the vertices of the fine and coarse grids.
*   **Performance:** On a standard PC with a 700MHz Pentium III processor, generating stitch cells for two levels of hierarchy (root and first level, both 32x32x32) took approximately 55ms.
For three levels (adding a second level with 12 grids of varying dimensions), it took approximately 340ms.
It preserves the original data values at the grid vertices.
It may require significant preprocessing to identify boundary elements and determine connections.
*   **When to use:** Use when crack-free visualization of AMR data is required and the AMR hierarchy has regular refinement ratios.
It is suitable for offline visualization or when the overhead of stitch cell generation is acceptable.
*   **When not to use:** Avoid if the AMR hierarchy has irregular refinement ratios or if real-time performance is critical and the overhead of stitch cell generation is too high.
It generalizes the 2D stitching approach to 3D, addressing the challenge of gaps between hierarchy levels in AMR data.
